title: DHCP Scope Exhaustion
exclusions: Measures address capacity only for the explicitly governed Windows DHCPv4 scopes returned by the designated authority server in each `capacity_domain_id`. It does not cover DHCPv6, non-Windows DHCP, rogue-server detection, DHCP service availability, relay reachability, DORA transaction success, option correctness, DNS registration, PXE/BOOTP capacity, policy-specific pools as independent denominators, lease churn, database integrity, failover replication health, or client-side address conflicts. `Get-DhcpServerv4ScopeStatistics -Failover` is the capacity authority; text audit-log code 14 and DHCP operational events 1063, 1376, 1377, and 20287 are corroborating symptoms, while audit code 13 means an address was found in use and is not scope exhaustion. Missing, incomplete, duplicate, stale, malformed, count-inconsistent, or mixed-policy snapshots are source-health failures and never healthy capacity. The example five-minute cadence, three-sample persistence, strict >90% utilization threshold, <=10-free-address floor, <=85% and >=20-free recovery conditions, and two-minute collection allowance are local policy choices, not Microsoft or Splunk defaults. This UC does not resize a subnet or scope, alter exclusions/reservations/lease duration, change a failover state, delete leases, restart DHCP, or attest compliance.
evidence: After deployment, retain the version-controlled `TA_windows_dhcp_capacity` collector and hash; its read-only execution identity and approved authority-server inventory; `dhcp_scope_policy.json` revision with capacity-domain, scope, failover, threshold, recovery, owner, and effective-time values; effective PowerShell/scripted-input and JSON parsing configuration; one complete manifest plus its exact scope rows for every alert sample; independent source-health output; the `windows_dhcp_scope_exhaustion` saved-search definition, ACL, schedule, dispatch history, and result rows; dashboard and alert-action revisions; same-time DHCP console or PowerShell comparisons; relevant `DhcpSrvLog` code 14 and DHCP Server event evidence; bounded exceptions; incident dispositions; and dated positive, negative, threshold-boundary, denominator, duplicate, missing-scope, stale, persistence, failover, and recovery tests. Result evidence must preserve the authority server, scope identity/state, policy ID, all three sample epochs, free/in-use/percentage values, thresholds, lowest free count, peak utilization, snapshot IDs, and indexing time. This documentation-only review created no DHCP, PowerShell, Splunk, dashboard, alert, or production evidence.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In an isolated index with fixed event and dispatch times, emit schema-1 five-minute snapshots for `capacity_domain_id=lab-dhcp-a`, authority `dhcp-lab-01`, policy `scope-capacity-v1`, and one active scope. For each of three consecutive `sample_epoch` values 300 seconds apart, emit exactly one complete manifest with `expected_scope_count=1` and one unique scope row. Use `addresses_in_use=9001`, `addresses_free=999`, and `percentage_in_use=90.01`, with thresholds 90% and 10 free, recovery values 85% and 20 free, and `required_consecutive_samples=3`; expect exactly one utilization result with three breach samples. Repeat with 10 in use, exactly 10 free, and 50% utilization; expect one `free_addresses` result because the free boundary is inclusive. Assert all identity, sample, threshold, peak, minimum, and use-case fields.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Run isolated variants and expect zero primary rows for each: utilization exactly 90% with 11 free addresses; 89.99% with exactly 11 free; only two breaches; breach/healthy/breach; three nonconsecutive samples; an inactive scope; no manifest; two manifests; `snapshot_complete=0`; expected count unequal to scope rows; duplicate authority/scope identity; two accepted snapshot IDs for one sample; a missing scope; wrong source, source type, schema, record type, or cadence; future, fractional, stale, or misaligned epochs; negative or fractional counts; zero denominator; percentage outside 0-100 or differing by more than 0.11 percentage point from counts; invalid thresholds; mixed policy values across the sequence; and a newest expected sample that is absent. A separate source-health search must report every rejected snapshot. For recovery, require three complete consecutive samples at or below 85% and at or above 20 free; a bounded exception may suppress delivery only after the base result and must not alter result count.

dataSources: Primary source: a deployment-owned Windows PowerShell collector runs Microsoft `Get-DhcpServerv4Scope` and `Get-DhcpServerv4ScopeStatistics -Failover` against one designated authority per logical capacity domain every five minutes and emits complete JSON snapshots to `index=windows`, `source=windows_dhcp_scope_capacity`, `sourcetype=ms:windows:dhcp:scope`. Extracted fields include `capacity_domain_id, authority_server, scope_id, scope_name, scope_state, addresses_free, addresses_in_use, percentage_in_use, sample_epoch, snapshot_id, policy_id`. Optional Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (Splunkbase 742) sources are `sourcetype=DhcpSrvLog` and XML DHCP Server event channels; they corroborate rejected leases and warnings but do not supply the current capacity denominator.
app: A version-controlled deployment app such as `TA_windows_dhcp_capacity` supplies the read-only PowerShell collector, policy, JSON parsing, complete-snapshot source-health search, primary saved search, recovery logic, dashboard, fixtures, and bounded exception lookup. Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (`Splunk_TA_windows`, Splunkbase 742) is optional for `DhcpSrvLog` knowledge and Windows DHCP event collection; it does not implement the custom scope-statistics snapshot, and the Universal Forwarder is transport software rather than a Splunkbase app.

description: Detects an active Windows DHCPv4 scope whose authoritative, complete statistics snapshot breaches either its percentage-used limit or absolute-free-address floor in three consecutive five-minute samples. It reconciles every snapshot manifest, scope count, identity, denominator, percentage, cadence, freshness, state, failover designation, and policy value before returning a capacity finding.
value: A depleted address pool prevents new or returning clients from obtaining usable network configuration even when the server process is running. Governed scope-level capacity trends provide time to reclaim or add addresses safely, while an absolute reserve floor catches small pools and complete-snapshot controls stop collection gaps or duplicated failover views from masquerading as trustworthy demand.
implementation: Deploy a signed `TA_windows_dhcp_capacity` collector on a qualified Windows management host or DHCP server. Designate one query authority per logical scope/failover capacity domain, join `Get-DhcpServerv4Scope` configuration to `Get-DhcpServerv4ScopeStatistics -Failover`, and emit one manifest plus one normalized scope row every five minutes. Save the primary SPL as `windows_dhcp_scope_exhaustion`, schedule it two minutes after each sample slot, and page only after three complete consecutive breaches of the governed >90% or <=10-free example policy. Operate missing-snapshot health, three-sample <=85% and >=20-free recovery, and DHCP audit/event corroboration separately.
visualization: Dashboard `Windows — DHCP Scope Capacity`: place expected authority/capacity domains with missing, late, incomplete, duplicate, malformed, or count-inconsistent snapshots first. Show active scopes above utilization threshold, at/below free-address floor, and breaching both; inactive scopes must be visibly separate. Provide a table with authority, scope ID/name, failover relationship, addresses in use/free, percentage, both alert thresholds, breach reason, three sample times, owner, forecast, and exception state. Add 24-hour and 30-day free-address/percentage trends; a heat map by scope and capacity domain; and gauges whose denominators come only from accepted statistics objects. Drill down to raw snapshot and manifest, the same-time `Get-DhcpServerv4ScopeStatistics -Failover` object, DHCP console **IPv4 > <scope> > Display Statistics**, scope configuration, reservations/exclusions/leases, failover state, `DhcpSrvLog` code 14, and DHCP Server events 1063/1376/1377/20287. Never render missing/rejected scope data as zero usage, unlimited free capacity, or green.
schema: Custom complete Windows DHCPv4 scope-statistics JSON snapshot
dataModelAcceleration: Not applicable to the primary alert. The Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows maps `DhcpSrvLog` lease activity to Network Sessions, but transaction rows and Change records do not provide the current `AddressesFree`, `AddressesInUse`, `PercentageInUse`, complete scope manifest, designated failover authority, or per-scope capacity policy. A purpose-built summary index may be used only if it preserves every accepted manifest, scope identity, sample epoch, count/denominator invariant, policy revision, and source-health failure and passes parity tests against raw events; generic `tstats count` is not scope utilization.

knownFalsePositives:
A returned row is a real sustained threshold breach in accepted Windows DHCP scope-statistics snapshots. It can still be expected, incorrectly governed, or less urgent than topology suggests; do not call the measurements fabricated merely because the business accepts the risk.

1. **Planned office, campus, event, or wireless-density surge** — A town hall, training week, return-to-office day, exam, conference, or device rollout can consume addresses predictably. Compare reservations, lease creation/renewal rates, access-point counts, event schedule, historical high-water mark, and remaining time-to-exhaustion. Adjust a named policy only after capacity ownership review; use an exact bounded notification exception for one approved event.

2. **Lease duration intentionally exceeds client presence** — Guest, mobile, VPN, lab, or imaging clients can leave while their leases remain valid, so `AddressesInUse` can exceed devices currently online. Compare configured lease duration, active leases, client population, and churn. Change lease duration only after DHCP/network impact review; never delete active leases automatically from this result.

3. **Reservations, exclusions, policies, or superscope design reduce the usable pool** — An operator may expect the raw subnet to contain more addresses than the server can actually lease. Microsoft scope statistics, not subnet arithmetic, remain authoritative for this detector. Inspect scope range, exclusions, reservations, policy ranges, superscope membership, and the exact rejected-client path before deciding the alert is benign.

4. **DHCP failover redistribution or partner maintenance** — In COMMUNICATION INTERRUPTED, PARTNER DOWN, recovery, or load-balance maintenance, per-partner free pools and ownership can look different from normal. The collector uses one designated authority with `-Failover` to avoid double counting, but a state transition can legitimately reduce immediately available capacity. Correlate relationship state, MCLT, partner health, this-server/partner pool fields, maintenance ticket, and client-request events; do not sum two independently collected logical-scope rows.

5. **Scope migration, split, merge, renumbering, or staged replacement** — Old and new scopes can coexist while clients move, and an old scope may remain highly occupied until leases expire. Verify VLAN/router-helper change, activation state, migration schedule, lease duration, rollback plan, and expected-scope manifest. Inactive rows do not page, but missing or duplicate scope identity must remain a source-health defect.

6. **Disaster-recovery or isolated standby DHCP server** — A replicated or restored server can hold stale-looking lease data while intentionally not serving clients. Confirm whether it is the governed capacity authority, its failover role, network isolation, restore timestamp, and activation procedure. Remove it from the authority inventory through versioned policy rather than broadly excluding its host name.

7. **Synthetic capacity exercise** — A lab or approved production-readiness test may create leases, narrow a disposable scope, or temporarily lower policy thresholds to prove alerting. Preserve exercise ID, scope, policy revision, start, exclusive expiry, owner, approver, and rollback evidence. Never perform destructive lease or scope changes in production solely to test this UC.

8. **Threshold policy is inappropriate for scope size or service objective** — Ten free addresses can be critical for a busy /24 and overly conservative for a nearly static tiny pool; 10% free in a very large range may provide ample lead time. Use both percentage and absolute floors plus burn-rate context, then govern per-scope values. Do not silently alter event fields or raise fleetwide thresholds to clear one alert.

9. **Address-conflict activity is mistaken for capacity** — `DhcpSrvLog` code 13 means an address was found in use, not that the pool is exhausted. Conflicts can mark addresses unusable and indirectly reduce capacity, but investigate BAD_ADDRESS leases, duplicate static assignments, conflict-detection settings, and network ownership separately. Code 14, event 1063, and event 20287 corroborate actual rejected allocation attempts.

**Safe notification suppression:** use lookup windows_dhcp_scope_capacity_exceptions.csv only after the base result. Key it by exact `capacity_domain_id,authority_server,scope_id,policy_id` and require numeric inclusive `valid_from_epoch`, exclusive `valid_until_epoch`, owner, approver, ticket, reason, and expected remediation. Reject wildcard scopes, whole-environment entries, host-only keys, open-ended dates, and exceptions for missing, partial, duplicate, stale, malformed, denominator-invalid, or mixed-policy telemetry. Preserve the finding and matched exception in a review index. Recovery requires three complete consecutive samples in which utilization is <= the policy recovery percentage and free addresses are >= its recovery floor.

detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and exact capacity contract

Assign accountable Windows DHCP, network/IPAM, Splunk collection/content, telemetry-health, service-desk, and incident owners. Inventory every Windows DHCPv4 server, scope, superscope, policy range, relay/VLAN, reservation/exclusion pattern, lease duration, and failover relationship. Define one stable `capacity_domain_id` for each independently evaluated logical authority and one designated `authority_server` for each logical scope. For a failover scope, query one governed member with `Get-DhcpServerv4ScopeStatistics -Failover`; do not poll both members and sum their aggregate rows. Microsoft documents that `-Failover` includes failover-related scope statistics, including local and partner pools. Preserve those component fields for diagnosis when present, but use the returned aggregate `AddressesFree`, `AddressesInUse`, and `PercentageInUse` as the primary capacity object.

Run the collector locally on a DHCP server or from a qualified Windows management host with the DHCP Server PowerShell module. Its service identity needs only the tested rights required to read scope configuration/statistics from approved targets and write output to its local Splunk input. It needs no permission to add/remove scopes, change lease duration, delete leases, force replication, change failover state, authorize a server, restart DHCP, or modify routing. Qualify the exact Windows Server, DhcpServer module, Universal Forwarder, PowerShell handler, add-on, parsing tier, and Splunk platform versions in nonproduction; this editorial review executed none.

Define a versioned `policy_id` per scope or group with identical operational requirements. The catalogue example alerts after three complete five-minute samples when `PercentageInUse` is strictly greater than 90 or `AddressesFree` is less than or equal to 10. Exactly 90% with 11 free is healthy; 90.01% breaches the percentage branch; exactly 10 free breaches the absolute branch. Microsoft shows >80% only as a cmdlet filtering example, not a universal alert threshold. Size policy from observed lease churn, lease duration, procurement/network lead time, subnet limits, redundancy, site criticality, and time-to-exhaustion. Recovery uses three complete samples at <=85% and >=20 free so an incident does not flap on the trigger boundary. Set per-scope values where small or very large pools make the examples inappropriate.

## Step 1 — Collect one atomic logical snapshot

Use `Get-DhcpServerv4Scope -ComputerName <authority>` to inventory configured scopes and state, then call `Get-DhcpServerv4ScopeStatistics -ComputerName <authority> -Failover` without an SPL-side reconstruction from lease events. Join by canonical `ScopeId` and require exactly one statistics object for every configured scope. Before coding against property names, inspect the actual object with `Get-Member` on every supported Windows version. Normalize only documented, observed properties. Never invent zero for a missing member, treat a command exception as an empty server, or derive the denominator from subnet mask alone; exclusions, reservations, policies, BAD_ADDRESS entries, and failover ownership affect usable capacity.

Create one five-minute scheduler slot `sample_epoch`, aligned to a multiple of 300 UTC seconds, one actual `snapshot_epoch`, and one UUID `snapshot_id`. Emit one compact JSON `scope` row for each configured IPv4 scope. Include stable capacity domain, authority, scope ID/name/state, aggregate free/in-use counts and percentage, normalized failover flag/relationship, policy ID, trigger/recovery thresholds, and required sample count. Counts must be nonnegative integers. Percentage must be finite and 0-100. The collector and SPL both reconcile it to `100*AddressesInUse/(AddressesFree+AddressesInUse)` within 0.11 percentage point to allow two-decimal display rounding. If the qualified object does not reconcile under that tolerance, record its raw members and fail the snapshot rather than silently changing arithmetic.

Buffer all scope rows and emit the `manifest` only after configuration and statistics calls, joins, normalizations, and validations succeed. `expected_scope_count` must equal emitted rows and distinct `(authority_server,scope_id)` identities. Set `snapshot_complete=1` only when every expected scope is present exactly once. A zero-scope authority is an inventory/configuration defect for this UC and cannot pass the search. On command failure, timeout, access denial, missing/duplicate statistics, invalid count, malformed policy, or partial stdout, emit a separately classified collector-health record and no complete manifest. Protect policy updates atomically, reject overlapping executions, and include code/policy revision in raw evidence.

The `scriptExample` is illustrative and intentionally sets nonfailover defaults; production code must join a governed failover inventory and map observed failover members rather than assuming `none`. It must also catch errors, prevent pipeline formatting output, use `Write-Output`, serialize one JSON object per line, and avoid localized display text. Do not collect MAC addresses or client names in this capacity feed; lease-level personal data belongs in restricted diagnostic sources only when justified.

## Step 2 — Configure Splunk transport and parsing

Package the signed collector in `TA_windows_dhcp_capacity`. A local PowerShell input on a Windows Splunk instance can use an app-owned stanza such as:

```ini
[powershell://windows_dhcp_scope_capacity]
script = . "$SplunkHome\etc\apps\TA_windows_dhcp_capacity\bin\collect-dhcp-capacity.ps1"
schedule = */5 * * * *
source = windows_dhcp_scope_capacity
sourcetype = ms:windows:dhcp:scope
index = windows
disabled = 0
```

Splunk documents that PowerShell input stdout is indexed and that the handler supports scheduled commands/scripts. On Splunk Cloud the script runs on a customer-managed Windows forwarder and forwards events; it does not run in the managed search tier. Validate the exact handler syntax on the qualified release. If one JSON line is not reliably one event, write complete lines atomically to a protected spool and monitor the completed file. Never edit an add-on's `default` directory.

Configure JSON search-time extraction and line breaking on the required parsing/search tiers:

```ini
[ms:windows:dhcp:scope]
SHOULD_LINEMERGE = false
LINE_BREAKER = ([\r\n]+)
KV_MODE = json
TRUNCATE = 16384
```

Set `TRUNCATE` from measured maximum row size. Confirm `_time` is the actual snapshot epoch or remains within 120 seconds of it, while `sample_epoch` remains the exact cadence slot. Verify effective settings with `splunk btool inputs list powershell://windows_dhcp_scope_capacity --debug` and `splunk btool props list ms:windows:dhcp:scope --debug`; inspect app assignment, service identity, script signature policy, index existence/RBAC, forwarding queues, JSON extraction, and duplicate stanzas.

## Step 3 — Establish source health before capacity paging

Maintain `windows_dhcp_capacity_inventory.csv` or an equivalent governed KV collection with capacity domain, authority, scope ID, failover relationship, expected state, policy ID, owner, enabled epoch, and retirement epoch. A dedicated search must report an expected authority or scope missing after one cadence plus measured indexing delay; no/multiple manifest; incomplete manifest; expected/event/distinct count mismatch; duplicate scope; tied snapshot IDs for one sample; unknown scope; authority or policy change; sample not aligned to 300 seconds; future/stale event; `_time` mismatch; wrong source/type/schema; invalid state/count/percentage/denominator; collector error; and a failover scope emitted independently by two authorities.

Route source health to DHCP and Splunk owners. Never turn a missing scope into zero use or a failed command into zero free addresses. The primary search deliberately rejects incomplete snapshots because silence cannot distinguish healthy capacity from an absent server. Dashboard source trust above utilization, and preserve `_indextime` to measure delay.

The search expects the latest slot at `floor((now()-120)/300)*300`, allowing two minutes after each five-minute boundary. Measure p99 collector runtime and indexing delay. Schedule the saved search after this allowance. If routine delay approaches two minutes, correct script duration, remote query, output queues, receivers, indexing, clock, or scheduling before widening the window. Update collector, SPL, tests, health search, runbook, and dashboard together if cadence changes.

## Step 4 — Create and understand the primary SPL

Save the sidecar `spl` verbatim as `windows_dhcp_scope_exhaustion` and trigger when result count is greater than zero. The base search fixes index, source, source type, schema, record types, and a bounded horizon. Numeric conversion prevents lexical comparisons. Epoch checks require integer five-minute slots, actual collection within two minutes of the slot, and event time within two minutes of collection.

For each scope row, the search creates a stable authority/scope identity, recomputes total and percentage, and validates state, failover designation, counts, percentage tolerance, policy identity, strict trigger/recovery ordering, and exactly three required samples. `eventstats` then requires one manifest, one set of manifest controls, complete flag one, and equality among expected, actual, valid, and distinct scope counts. It rejects two accepted snapshot IDs for the same capacity-domain slot. Every rejected condition belongs in source health.

The dual threshold is an OR: percentage strictly above policy or free count at/below policy. An active-sample gate prevents an inactive scope from paging. After deterministic sorting, `streamstats window=3` requires three complete active breaches, unchanged threshold/recovery/sample policy, slots exactly 600 seconds from first to last, and the newest expected slot. This rejects two-sample spikes, breach/healthy/breach, sparse history, policy drift, stale older runs, and a missing latest snapshot. The result retains latest raw counts plus peak percentage and lowest free count across persistence.

Do not replace the detector with `DhcpSrvLog | stats dc(IP_Address)`: log events are transactions within a search window, not current leases or a denominator, and one client can renew repeatedly. Audit code 13 is conflict detection; code 14 is a rejected lease because the pool is exhausted. DHCP events 1063 (scope/superscope full), 1376/1377 (low-address warnings), and 20287 (client request dropped because applicable ranges are out of addresses) are excellent incident evidence but can be absent before a risk threshold and do not enumerate all current free capacity.

Implement recovery in stateful incident handling, not by negating the trigger. Require three consecutive accepted samples for the same identity/policy with percentage <= recovery threshold and free addresses >= recovery floor. Missing data cannot recover an incident. Throttle by exact `capacity_domain_id,authority_server,scope_id,policy_id`, preserve every evaluation, and reopen if either trigger branch persists.

## Step 5 — Collect corroborating Microsoft DHCP evidence correctly

The Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows identifies `DhcpSrvLog` as Microsoft DHCP Server log information and maps supported transaction codes to Network Sessions. Monitor the configured DHCP audit-log path, commonly `%windir%\System32\Dhcp`, only after testing rotation, headers, character encoding, source identity, and current add-on extraction. Restrict access because rows can contain client IP, host, MAC, user, vendor class, and relay information. Search numeric ID/code and parsed fields, not localized `Description` text.

Microsoft's archived audit-log documentation defines code 13 as “IP address found in use” and code 14 as “lease request could not be satisfied because the address pool of the scope was exhausted.” Treat 14 as rejected-client corroboration and 13 as a separate conflict/BAD_ADDRESS diagnostic. Neither contains a current scope denominator. Monitor audit-log health events such as append/path failures separately so absence of code 14 is not treated as proof that clients were served.

Collect **Applications and Services Logs > Microsoft > Windows > DHCP-Server** XML channels where supported and preserve provider, channel, event ID, version, scope payload, server, and rendered message. Microsoft lists 1063 scope/superscope full, 1376 residual range percentage/free warning, 1377 superscope warning, and 20287 client request dropped due to exhausted applicable ranges/policy ranges. Confirm payload fields on each Windows Server build; do not write brittle regex against English message order. These events can identify impact and policy/superscope nuances that the aggregate scope row needs during triage.

For failover, preserve relationship state and this-server/partner free/in-use components returned with `-Failover`. COMMUNICATION INTERRUPTED and PARTNER DOWN have different service implications; a member can have a constrained local pool while aggregate relationship capacity remains different. Do not add per-member totals twice. Run separate failover-health monitoring for replication queue, state transitions, partner reachability, MCLT, and rejected updates; capacity alone does not prove redundancy health.

## Step 6 — Validate data, boundaries, persistence, and Windows behavior

Use isolated indexes with fixed epochs and the exact `controlTest` fixtures. Assert one manifest and one scope row per snapshot; exact output identity; 300-second cadence; a 600-second three-sample span; >90 versus exactly 90; <=10 versus 11; both-branch reason; inactive state; source freshness; duplicate rejection; policy stability; and recovery. Test integer totals that reconcile to 90.01 exactly, two-decimal rounding within 0.11, and a mismatch outside tolerance. Test zero total, negative/fractional counts, NaN/infinite serialization rejection, percentages below zero/above 100, and scope names with Unicode.

On a nonproduction DHCP server, compare collector output at the same instant with:

```powershell
Get-DhcpServerv4Scope -ComputerName dhcp-lab-01
Get-DhcpServerv4ScopeStatistics -ComputerName dhcp-lab-01 -Failover
```

In DHCP Manager inspect **IPv4 > <scope> > Display Statistics**, scope state, address pool, exclusions, reservations, address leases, policies, superscope, and failover properties. Record command time and accept that leases can change between observations; compare inside a bounded interval. Verify actual object properties with `Get-Member`, and qualify standalone, load-balance, and hot-standby scopes. Confirm one logical failover scope is not counted twice.

Generate threshold fixtures in Splunk rather than exhausting a production pool. If runtime testing needs real DHCP behavior, create a disposable isolated lab scope and clients under network change control. Prove audit code 14 and events 1063/1376/1377/20287 only where the Windows build and lab condition legitimately emit them. Never shorten a production scope, delete leases, consume addresses, change failover state, or block a partner merely to test monitoring.

Measure collection runtime, CPU, remote-call load, output bytes, indexing delay, search runtime, and event/log volume at fleet scale. Keep `status=draft` until exact Windows/module/add-on/Splunk versions, permissions, policy inventory, complete-snapshot behavior, source health, failover identity, fixtures, alert delivery, dashboard, recovery, suppression expiry, and responder runbook are accepted by accountable DHCP, network, and Splunk owners.

## Step 7 — Operationalize response, suppression, and evidence

Build the dashboard described in `visualization`, use UTC or label timezone, and show source health before capacity state. Add a burn-rate forecast only after enough clean history exists; expose its method and confidence and never let it replace the deterministic floor. Severity depends on current free addresses, consumption rate, rejected clients, site/service criticality, alternate DHCP capacity, failover health, and remediation lead time. One scope at 91% with hundreds free is not equivalent to a small scope with zero free.

Alert text should say: `Windows DHCPv4 scope sustained capacity breach for 15 minutes: <authority>/<scope>`. Include both current counts, percentage, branch, thresholds, peak/minimum, three UTC sample times, policy, failover relationship/state context, source health, owner, exceptions, code-14/1063/1376/1377/20287 counts, and runbook.

Responder sequence:
1. Verify exact capacity domain/authority/scope/policy, complete manifests, three consecutive slots, denominator reconciliation, no duplicate authority, and no bounded exception.
2. Run the same `Get-DhcpServerv4ScopeStatistics -Failover` query and open Display Statistics; preserve timestamped output.
3. Confirm scope active state, pool/range, exclusions, reservations, BAD_ADDRESS entries, policies, superscope, current leases, duration, relay/VLAN, and recent network/DHCP changes.
4. Check `DhcpSrvLog` code 14 and DHCP events 1063/1376/1377/20287 for actual rejection, plus audit-log and collector health. Treat code 13 as conflict evidence, not exhaustion proof.
5. Inspect failover relationship state, partner reachability, local/partner free pools, replication, MCLT, and whether alternate servers can serve the affected clients.
6. Choose a reviewed remediation: reclaim invalid reservations/exclusions or stale/BAD_ADDRESS causes where safe, adjust lease policy, expand an address pool within the existing subnet, add a routed subnet/superscope, re-subnet, or move clients. Coordinate routers, relays, DNS, NAC, firewalls, and endpoint configuration as required.
7. Validate client allocation through an approved lab/affected-client test, same-time statistics, no new rejected-request events, and three complete recovery samples.

Never automatically delete leases/reservations, shrink or expand a scope, change subnet mask, alter exclusions/policies/options, reduce lease duration, authorize/deauthorize DHCP, change failover state, force replication, restart the service, or reconfigure relays from this alert. Microsoft notes that expanding host capacity can require coordinated re-subnetting; an unreviewed change can create duplicate addresses or routing failure.

Apply only the exact bounded lookup contract in `knownFalsePositives`. Suppress notification, not the base result or source-health search. Review capacity domains, scope inventory, designated authorities, failover mapping, thresholds/recovery, lease duration, owner, exceptions, collector versions/permissions, and dashboard quarterly and after subnet, VLAN, DHCP, failover, Windows, Splunk, or organizational changes.

## Step 8 — Troubleshoot without converting unknown state to capacity

- **No primary results:** check expected-authority/source health, input schedule, script signature and identity, DhcpServer module, remote permissions, target resolution, forwarding queues, index routing, and JSON parsing. No results do not prove free addresses exist.
- **Access denied or RPC/CIM failure:** run the exact cmdlet under the collection identity, verify approved remote-management path and least-privilege read rights, and emit an incomplete run. Do not grant broad DHCP administration merely to hide a collection design fault.
- **Manifest count mismatch:** compare `Get-DhcpServerv4Scope` with statistics output, policy filters, mid-run scope changes, script exceptions, duplicate stdout, and truncation. Retry the next slot; do not lower expected count after partial collection.
- **Percentage does not reconcile:** inspect raw object properties/types, rounding, policy-specific/failover semantics, module version, and same-time GUI values. Preserve raw evidence and qualify the version before changing tolerance.
- **Duplicate scope in failover:** correct authority inventory and `capacity_domain_id`; do not `dedup` arbitrary partners or sum both aggregate rows.
- **Scope missing after migration:** confirm state, authority, policy effective/retired epoch, deployment consistency, and source-health inventory. Version the manifest intentionally; never let disappearance mean recovery.
- **Code 14 or event 20287 occurs below aggregate threshold:** inspect DHCP policies, superscope selection, excluded/reserved/BAD_ADDRESS ranges, relay/client subnet, failover local pool, and event payload. A policy-specific range can be exhausted while the aggregate scope has free addresses; design a separate policy-pool detector if needed.
- **Code 13 spikes:** investigate conflicts, static assignments, duplicate clients, BAD_ADDRESS leases, and conflict detection. Do not count code 13 as a capacity threshold.
- **GUI and snapshot differ:** match authority, scope, failover mode, query time, and aggregate versus per-partner fields; lease activity between observations is expected. Preserve bounded timestamps.
- **Alert flaps:** verify policy stability, exact boundary operators, cadence, identity, and three-sample recovery hysteresis. Do not close on one healthy sample or missing data.
- **`DhcpSrvLog` fields are null:** verify current file header/format, monitor stanza, source type spelling/case, add-on knowledge placement, rotation, and event-code extraction. Keep the custom statistics snapshot primary.
- **CIM/tstats is empty:** expected for capacity. Network Sessions represents DHCP transactions, not a complete current scope denominator.
grandmaExplanation: We check how many network addresses each Windows server can still hand out. If a pool stays nearly full or has only a few addresses left, we warn the team before new phones, laptops, or other devices are turned away.
hardware: Windows Server systems running the Microsoft DHCP Server role, or qualified Windows management hosts with the DHCP Server PowerShell module and read access to designated Windows DHCPv4 authorities. DHCPv6, non-Windows servers, managed network services, appliances, disconnected authorities, and logical scopes without one governed failover-aware query authority require a separate collection and identity contract.

```powershell
# Illustrative collector core; production code must add policy validation, error handling,
# complete-manifest semantics, non-overlap, signing, and tests.
$Authority = 'dhcp01.contoso.example'
$CapacityDomain = 'campus-a-dhcp'
$PolicyId = 'scope-capacity-v1'
$SampleEpoch = [int64]([Math]::Floor([DateTimeOffset]::UtcNow.ToUnixTimeSeconds() / 300) * 300)
$SnapshotEpoch = [DateTimeOffset]::UtcNow.ToUnixTimeSeconds()
$SnapshotId = [guid]::NewGuid().ToString()
$Scopes = @(Get-DhcpServerv4Scope -ComputerName $Authority -ErrorAction Stop)
$Stats = @(Get-DhcpServerv4ScopeStatistics -ComputerName $Authority -Failover -ErrorAction Stop)
$Rows = foreach ($Scope in $Scopes) {
  $Stat = $Stats | Where-Object { $_.ScopeId.IPAddressToString -eq $Scope.ScopeId.IPAddressToString }
  if (@($Stat).Count -ne 1) { throw "Missing or duplicate statistics for $($Scope.ScopeId)" }
  [ordered]@{
    schema_version=1; record_type='scope'; capacity_domain_id=$CapacityDomain
    authority_server=$Authority.ToLowerInvariant(); sample_epoch=$SampleEpoch
    snapshot_id=$SnapshotId; snapshot_epoch=$SnapshotEpoch
    scope_id=$Scope.ScopeId.IPAddressToString; scope_name=[string]$Scope.Name
    scope_state=$Scope.State.ToString().ToLowerInvariant()
    addresses_free=[int64]$Stat.AddressesFree; addresses_in_use=[int64]$Stat.AddressesInUse
    percentage_in_use=[double]$Stat.PercentageInUse
    failover_enabled=0; failover_relationship='none'; policy_id=$PolicyId
    utilization_threshold_pct=90.0; free_address_threshold=10
    recovery_utilization_pct=85.0; recovery_free_addresses=20
    required_consecutive_samples=3
  }
}
$Rows | ForEach-Object { $_ | ConvertTo-Json -Compress }
[ordered]@{schema_version=1;record_type='manifest';capacity_domain_id=$CapacityDomain;sample_epoch=$SampleEpoch;snapshot_id=$SnapshotId;snapshot_epoch=$SnapshotEpoch;snapshot_complete=1;expected_scope_count=$Rows.Count;max_snapshot_age_minutes=17} | ConvertTo-Json -Compress
```
